name: Local Custody Workflow Provenance
text:
Custody is not an execution history. Kifor and coauthors study agent-mediated healthcare systems in which data, procedures, and logs are divided among heterogeneous autonomous information systems. They show that provenance-aware instrumentation can record events, dependencies, and human decisions across those systems. The resulting process documentation represents the distributed execution, connects its causal steps, and permits later reconstruction and audit. This independently extends Kaal's failure claim: custody identifies where the bytes reside, but a separate recording architecture must preserve what the composed services did.

The evidence is a 2006 peer-reviewed healthcare systems article. Its agents coordinate medical services, not sovereign local LLM runtimes. The paper does not test whether any current local runtime preserves a sufficient history or whether provenance alone creates institutional accountability. One design requirement follows. Composed services need execution-time provenance before custody can answer what happened.

sourceProvenance.sourceProposition: Kifor and coauthors show that data, workflow steps, and logs in agent-mediated healthcare can remain distributed across heterogeneous autonomous systems. A separate provenance layer records events, causal dependencies, participating services, and human decisions during execution so that the process can later be reconstructed and audited.

sourceEvidencePassages.text: Provenance is an innovative approach to trace events in complex distributed processes, dependencies between such events, and associated decisions by human actors.

In the case of distributed medical applications, the data (containing the healthcare history of a single patient), the workflow (of the procedures carried out on that patient) and the logs (recording meaningful events in those procedures) are distributed among several heterogeneous and autonomous information systems.

Making electronic systems provenance aware [2] enables users to trace how a particular result has been arrived at by identifying the individual and aggregated services that produced a particular output.

By transforming a MAS into a provenance-aware MAS, the resulting system gets the capability to produce at execution-time an explicit representation of the distributed processes that are taking place (see example in Section 3).
